steps.title: Convert people into work rate
steps.content: If one worker completes a job in d days, the worker's daily rate is 1/d. For equally efficient workers, multiply the number of workers by the individual rate.
steps.example: One worker takes 12 days. Three equally efficient workers take 12/3 = 4 days.

steps.title: Use the men-days relationship
steps.prompt: 6 workers finish a job in 8 days. How many days would 12 equally efficient workers take?
steps.explanation: Total work = 6×8 = 48 worker-days. With 12 workers, time = 48/12 = 4 days.

steps.title: Account for working hours
steps.content: When daily hours differ, total work is proportional to workers × days × hours per day × efficiency. Compare the products rather than only the number of people.
steps.example: 4 workers for 5 days at 6 hours/day produce 120 worker-hours.

steps.title: Compare efficiencies
steps.prompt: 8 workers finish a task in 6 days at 5 hours/day. How many days do 10 equally efficient workers need at 4 hours/day?
steps.explanation: Work = 8×6×5 = 240 worker-hours. New daily capacity = 10×4 = 40 worker-hours. Days = 240/40 = 6. Correction: option C is correct.

steps.title: Handle alternating work
steps.content: When workers or pipes operate in turns, calculate the amount of work completed in each interval. Add the fractions until the total reaches one job, then account for any final partial interval.
steps.tip: Keep the unit of work consistent: one whole job or an LCM-based number of work units.

questions.prompt: 10 workers finish a job in 9 days. How many worker-days are required?
15 workers can complete a task in 12 days. How long would 20 equally efficient workers take?
If the number of equally efficient workers doubles, the time for the same job becomes:
questions.explanation: For fixed work, workers and time are inversely proportional.
